speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to move a motion under Standing Order 43. This permits me to make a brief statement concerning the purpose of the motion. It arises out of the publication yesterday of a letter from the office of President Nixon indicating that the restriction on the import of Canadian oil into the United States is definitely related to the insistence of the United States government on a continental energy policy. In view of the fact that this involves very serious implications in respect of the oil and gas industry in Canada I would move, seconded by the hon. member for York South:
That at four o'clock today the business for private members' hour be suspended, and that the House debate the serious situation arising out of the letter from President Nixon's office published yesterday, this debate, notwithstanding the provisions for adjourning the House, to continue for not more than three hours.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Bill
C-99 is perfectly drawn as far as procedure is concerned. In fact, it looks as though the minister has made an exact copy of that bill, with the exception of one change. He put in a new minimum wage of $1.65 an hour instead of a minimum wage of $2 an hour, as set out in Bill C-99, which as I say has been before the House in my name since last October.
I shall come in a few moments to my arguments as to why $1.65 an hour is not an adequate figure to be introducing at this time, but may I first point out that the alleged dislocations than this bill might create are really very minimal. According to such figures as I have been able to obtain, there are about 550,000 workers in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. These are workers in such industries as the railways and transportation generally, in the communications field, in banks and a number of other fields.
I am told, however, that something of the order of 10,000, perhaps fewer, of these employees are presently earning less than $1.65 an hour. In other words, this bill, asking for a minimum wage of $1.65 an hour, will affect only about 2 per cent of those employees under federal labour jurisdiction, which is an infinitesimal percentage of the total work force in Canada, at least so far as the direct application of this bill is concerned.
Therefore, what we are concerned with in this bill is a matter of principle, as well as the whole question of giving a lead to the provinces and to the economy of this country generally. I know the Minister of Labour is not happy with the bill. That was pretty obvious from the take-it-easy manner in which he presented the bill this morning and also from the effort that he made to say that this figure had been arrived at scientifically. When a figure of $1.65 has been arrived at scientifical-

ly, then I suggest this is a word we should look at. He did not say in that paragraph of his remarks what he meant, but to be fair to him I think I know what he had in mind.
Earlier in his remarks he made a statement, with which I thoroughly agree, on a matter I have spoken about a good many times on the floor of the House, namely that it is not enough to talk about increasing wages or pensions on the basis only of the increase that takes place in the cost of living index. This is a popular notion with which we have to deal all the time. Many people, even many who are affected, think that if only they can get their incomes or their pensions geared to the cost of living index, all will be well.
The fact of the matter is-the Minister of Labour in fact said so this morning-that this approach is not good enough. All you have when a wage or a pension is indexed by the rise in the cost of living is a scheme that keeps you in the same position that you were before relative to the goods and services that are available. But this can actually depress your position with respect to that of other workers and members of society. I am happy to see the Minister of Labour nodding his head up and down, and also his parliamentary secretary, which shows that there are two members at least on the government benches who agree with me. When one considers the fact that any indexing the government has done has not only been confined to the cost of living figures but has also been put under a 2 per cent ceiling per year, then it becomes a bit of a hoax. So I agree with the Minister of Labour that we must look at other statistics when we talk about indexing such a factor, as the minimum wage.
o (2:10p.m.)
The minister spoke about an average wage and wage increases in other sectors of the economy. He also referred of course to the wage index. I do not know whether this morning he referred to the fact that the wage index is used in one or two other places, notably in the Canada Pension Plan, but whether or not he did I shall mention it now. The wage index is used in the Canada Pension Plan in computing the pension a person will receive under that legislation up to the point of retirement. Even in that legislation, however, those who have retired have their pensions indexed only according to the rise in the cost of living. But in this one place in federal legislation, namely in respect of the earlier stages of the Canada Pension Plan, we
May 29. 1970	COMMONS
do have a recognition that there is something better than the cost of living index, namely the wage index.
While I regret that this bill does not include some provision for automatic increases in the amount of the minimum wage, I would rather not have it at all than have one of these arrangements that is geared to the cost of living index with the kind of ceiling this government can place on such legislation. Nevertheless, it is still regrettable that the minister was not able to persuade his colleagues that this is the time to accept the principle of escalating the amount of the minimum wage on the basis of a concept or a formula that is fair. I take it that because the minister took his stand on this principle-a principle with which I agree-he wants me to believe, and I do believe him, that when he said he arrived at the figure of $1.65 on a scientific basis he means he arrived at it not only by looking at increases in the cost of living since the $1.25 was established but also by looking at other things such as the wage index and so on. That is fine, but how fair was the $1.25 minimum wage when it was established?
Any statistical computation that suggests that $1.65 today is as good in terms of purchasing power or wages as $1.25 was a few years ago does not face up to the fact that $1.25 was not sufficient at that time. What really bothers me about this kind of thing is that it goes on all the time in our society. We are trying to improve things for everybody but we always make much greater improvements for those in the middle and upper brackets than we do for those in the lower brackets. We justify this sometimes by using the percentage formula. So, if we give a 5 per cent increase to those in the upper brackets we say we will give only the same 5 per cent increase to those in the lower brackets. This goes on all the time, and the result is that we are forever widening the gap in our society between those at the bottom and those at the top. As I have said frequently this goes on not only in our society but in the world at large. All the things we do by way of external aid are pretty well nullified by the fact that the gap between the developing and the developed countries keeps getting wider and wider.
I think some day we must come to an era in our country where we concentrate not on doing things across the board to make sure those at the top receive their increases but where we concentrate on those at the bottom of the scale. This is the reason I would have

As I have said before, I believe one of the main improvements we made when we changed our rules a few years ago was the introduction of the report stage. It will be possible for us at that point-and I give notice now that I shall be doing so-to bring in an amendment to change the figure from $1.65 to $2 an hour. The advantage of an amendment of this type at the report stage is that one does not have to say that the bill be not now read. One does not have to take any negative action. One can just make the positive point by itself that the figure be $2 an hour rather than $1.65 an hour. I plead with members on all sides of the House, who after all are favourable to increases of various kinds, to support the proposition that these people at the bottom of the economic ladder in our country should receive more than is involved in the increase from $1.25 to $.1.65 an hour.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) made some reference to dislocations that any increase in the minimum wage might bring about. We agree with his statement that these dislocations should not deter us from acting in the way proposed or even more so. The hon.

The Economic Council of Canada puts the poverty line today at about $4,200 a year for a family. second reading debate. Come on, Mr. Minister-I know we are not supposed to talk that way here but other members do it so why can I not look him in the eye too and say to him, come on, Mr. Minister. It is always good to get improvements in labour legislation. I have been bringing in bills and making speeches on labour code matters for a quarter of a century or so and it is always a red letter day when some pro-

gress is made. The $1.65 an hour is better than $1.25, so this is a red letter day. But why not make it a really worthwhile day and come all the way with a bill that goes at least to $2 an hour?

speechtext: Here we have an important piece of legislation. The minister made it clear in his speech this morning that he wishes it were a lot better. Here is his chance. Mr. Speaker, upon reading Bill C-214, I can easily see that it is meant to change the minimum wage.
Naturally, the Canadian Labour Code could be improved with regard to industrial security and protection of young workers under 17 years of age.
However, what we are dealing with now is an amendment to the provisions of the Canadian Labour Code with regard to the minimum wage.
In businesses under federal jurisdiction, the hourly minimum wage will be raised from $1.25 to $1.65 if the bill before us is passed. The adjustment of 40 cents an hour is necessary and I do not know who could oppose it.
The measure will mostly benefit employees in broadcasting and shipping. It is normal that workers who are not protected under collective bargaining should get decent wages. It would also be appropriate if the minimum wage were revised regularly so as to correspond to the economic reality. I am convinced that the minister is keeping a close watch on this aspect of the problem.
Since the minimum wage was set at $1.25 an hour in 1965, it is obvious that an adjustment is necessary in 1970. However, a survey
May 29, 1970

Increase in Minimum Hourly Wage of minimum wage rates in the various provinces of Canada reveals that British Columbia, for instance, has a minimum wage rate of $1.50 an hour as compared with $1.40 in Alberta-it will be boosted to $1.55 next October 1. In Manitoba, the minimum rate is $1.35 and will be increased to $1.50 next October 1. In Quebec, it is now set at $1.35 in Montreal and $1.30 elsewhere in the province. I have noticed that in some other provinces there is a difference between urban and rural rates, in my opinion, this is not normal. In Ontario, the minimum wage is $1.30 an hour. As for Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia, they have two minimum rates, a $1.25 urban rate and a $1.15 rural rate. Their minimum wage for women is $1.00 in towns and 90 cents in rural areas.
Prince Edward Island applies a minimum rate of $1.25 for men and 90 cents for women, and in New Brunswick the minimum rate is $1.15.
Nova Scotia has the lowest minimum rate, $1.10 for men and 85 cents for women.
We feel that the change to the minimum wage brought about through Bill C-214 will set a practical example to all those whose responsibility it is to take decisions in this field.
e (2:30 p.m.)

I have been looking forward to the opportunity to say a few words on the Bill C-214, Mr. Speaker, mainly because of the importance I attach to the responsibility of Parliament to make sure that the Canadian worker receives a just and equitable wage for his labours. I wish to commend the minister for bringing in the legislation which, although delayed is still welcome. If I am not in error, I believe this is the first piece of legislation to be introduced by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). This is not through any fault of his. He was unable to lead earlier legislation through the House because of illness in his family. We all understood that and I am sure we are glad to see him back in the House after his recent visit to the hospital. We hope he will have his health restored so that he can continue to fight against the millionaires row in the cabinet on issues like this and can bring in some really good legislation.
I hope that the next legislation will be of greater value than this and much more important. However, this is a step in the right direction.
The minister mentioned that the academic economists take a dim view of minimum wages in this country but possibly they never had to work for $1.25 a day and therefore the subject does not bother them too much. I fully agree with the minister's comments that there were some misgivings about the minimum wage being uniform across the country, and I listened with interest to his dissertation in that area. He should realize, however, there are a lot of hard-nosed men, some of them in his cabinet, who have never worked, far less worked for $1.25 an hour. I think he should use his persuasive powers on them, as he is a persuasive minister and there is no question that he has worked very hard on this bill.
The minister mentioned that some people think that the raising of the minimum wage will put certain plants or firms out of business. I agree with his comment that if they are unable to work efficiently enough to pay the minimum wage then certainly they should be out of business. Of course, we should keep in mind the effect that the white paper may have on small businesses. We hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will not go forward with his measures in that particular field because it will certainly affect many small businesses.
As has already been mentioned, Mr. Speaker, this legislation covers approximately 532,000 government employees or those interwoven with government, and this is a small portion of the work force of the country. The minister also mentioned that in Toronto, a man with four children can draw $53 a week on welfare. Even with this increase in the minimum wage, he can only earn $66 a week so it is not a great step forward, though we are grateful for it.
There are two reasons why I have been anxious to enter the debate on this bill, Mr. Speaker, and if my second reason appears to contradict the first, it is because the bill is so typical of the legislation often proposed by the present government. There is an expression we use in the Maritimes that is familiar to members from other parts of the country: "You're darned if you do and you're darned if you don't." This expression applies to every bill that we have been asked to debate in recent months, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is time the government took the time and the trouble to examine the problems we are facing before it proposes the answers.
Over and over again, we are asked to consider legislation that is designed to solve a

vital problem, and then when we read the bill it is immediately apparent that no one in the government has taken the time or the trouble to make a thorough analysis of problems they are attempting to solve. I say that they are attempting to solve problems because I feel charitable at this moment. I want this government to continue to think of me as a friend. I want them to think of me as an understanding colleague, someone they can turn to for sympathy and a kind word as they drift around aimlessly trying to keep out of each other's way.
I must confess that at times I am moved to laughter, Mr. Speaker, such as is resounding in this chamber at the moment, but I want to assure my friends across the floor that it is not malicious laughter. In fairness to my friends squirming around on the government benches-or maybe mooing-I must admit that the technique works. I hear another sheep over there whimpering. We are dealing with people, Canadian People, who expect us to come up with solutions to serious problems, not stop-gap measures.
Before I deal with the deficiencies in Bill C-214, Mr. Speaker, and before I offer constructive criticism as to how this problem might have been handled, I would like to say that I am in favour of this bill as I have already intimated. tain standards for hours of work. The then minister of labour urged us to co-operate in passing the legislation quickly so that the living standards of the 500,000 workers under the federal jurisdiction would be protected. Employers were given an opportunity to appeal against the implementation of the minimum hours of work provisions as it applied to their industry. When some of us protested at that time we were told that we ought not to worry or protest very much because there had to be a transitional period. The government, the minister and the department were given a year in which to bring all industry under the provisions of the act. We have a situation which is a disgrace. I think I am right in saying that railway workers still are not covered by the 40-hour work week provision of this act. The present minister was once a railway employee. How long is he going to permit this to go on? It has gone on too long. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I remember a former minister of labour, now the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia, appealing to this House to pass the Canada Labour (Safety) Code without debate. He wanted to begin immediately protecting the rights, working and safety conditions of the workers who came under the federal jurisdictiion. He wanted that bill passed with no debate whatsoever. I understand that the safety regulations under that act have only been applied to the workers who came under the Devco operation.
The railway workers of Canada still do not have the protection which they would have if they were under provincial jurisdiction. There are no standards for the heating facili-

Under this bill the minimum wage for employees under federal jurisdiction will be raised from $1.25 an hour, which was set five years ago, to $1.65 an hour. I am sure the minister is aware that the Economic Council of Canada has set the poverty line for a family of four at $4,200 a year. I have made some rough calculations. I admit my arithmetic is not the best but my calculations show that $1.65 an hour, 40 hours a week, 52 weeks of the year amounts to between $3,300 and $3,400 a year. That is $700 or $800 below the poverty line set by the Economic Council of Canada. The minister and the government ought to be ashamed of this proposal.
The minister must have read the brief prepared by the Department of Labour. He must know that organization. This brief was submitted to the special Senate Committee on Poverty on May 22, 1969. Possibly someone else wrote this brief and the minister simply read it into the record, if he even did that. I wish to quote from page 248 of the committee evidence where the department's submission to the Senate committee is set out:
One should hope that minimum wage rates should be maintained at levels that will enable workers to support their families and maintain their health, dignity, efficiency and self-respect.

How do humanitarian considerations affect minimum wages? Will this objective be achieved by fixing the minimum wage at $1.65 an hour? I suggest it will not. I can see no reason for this figure except the refusal of the government in this as in nearly every other case to fight entrenched interests which are simply not prepared to pay an adequate wage.
The government has calculated that not more than 10,000 people who come under federal jurisdiction will be affected by this proposal. Most of the employees concerned are in industries which have been organized by trade unions and, as the minister has stated, they have long since been able to raise their wages to substantially more than $1.65 an hour. So the new rate will have little effect on federal employees. Even had the rate been fixed at $2.00 an hour, few employees under federal jurisdiction would have been affected, I submit-perhaps with the exception of some working in banks and in grain milling.
One of the good effects of the legislation passed five years ago, when we set the rate at $1.25 an hour, was that it acted as a spur to the provinces and encouraged them to increase their minimum wage rates. There are thousands, perhaps hundreds of thousands, of employees under provincial jurisdiction who receive less than the federal minimum wage-people who work in hotels, in service industries, in the garment industry; people who do housework, people who operate elevators, and so on. When the rate of $1.25 an hour was set five years ago we were doing something not only for federal employees but for workers under provincial jurisdiction.
This bill to raise the minimum wage to $1.65 an hour does virtually nothing to set an example for provincial authorities to follow. What is the situation? In British Columbia the minimum wage is already $1.50 an hour; in Alberta it is $1.50 and it will be $1.55 on October 1; in Manitoba, the rate is now $1.35 and this will increase to $1.55 on October 1. In Ontario the rate is $1.30; $1.50 in the construction industry. Quebec has a Montreal area rate of $1.35 effective from May 1 but this will be increased to $1.50 or more in the months to come. So we are not really doing anything, as we did last time, to set an example for the provinces, and I say this ought to be done.
The minister was urging my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre to persuade the

government of Manitoba to raise the minimum wage in that province. I think he knows better than that. I think he knows that the government of Manitoba would be happy to raise the minimum wage, but, like any other provincial government it has to face the probability that if it raises the minimum wage higher than the minimum in other provinces, particularly neighbouring provinces, certain types of industry which traditionally pay low wages will migrate. The government of Manitoba is no different in this sense from any other government. The way to bring about an increase in the minimum wage in the provinces is to set the federal minimum wage at a point which gives the provinces a reason for raising theirs. This is what happened last time, and it is what should be happening now.
There is one further point I wish to make; I do not intend to go into it in any great detail today. It is that neither the rate of $1.65 an hour or even the rate of $2 an hour suggested by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre would be sufficient to meet the problem of poverty which is faced by so many people in this country. Poverty is of various types. There are the working poor who will be affected by an increase in the minimum wage; the hundreds of thousands who make less than $1.65 an hour will be affected by a general increase in the minimum wage. But there are hundreds of thousands who are not working at all-old age pensioners, veterans, people who are ill and incapacitated. There are hundreds of thousands of Indians and Metis people who have never been able to find a place in our work-oriented economy.
I noticed an article written by James Gray in one of the Calgary newspapers; I believe it appeared as a reprint in the Ottawa Journal yesterday. It contained an estimate that 90 per cent of the 10,000 Indian people who have moved into Calgary are now living on welfare. For them an increase of this type in the minimum wage is of no benefit at all. What is needed is a redistribution of income. What we need, in fact, is a social security policy to guarantee every Canadian citizen an annual minimum income.

Health and Welfare, would have been completed, published and discussed by the people of Canada, as a result of which would have come forth government legislation or at least a statement of policy to the effect that in the not too distant future we would enact a law to guarantee to every person in Canada that they would not fall below a certain minimum standard of living. It is locked away in the cabinet because it is obvious that the cabinet is divided on the matter: it is divided between the view of ministers like the Minister of Labour, who I hope wants to do the right thing, and the view of ministers like the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) who are wedded to the illusion that the way to deal with inflation is to have more unemployed and to put the lid on improvements to the pension plan, whether for old age pensioners or veterans. there is no doubt it is inadequate-or should we vote for it simply because it is better than the present rate of $1.25? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the hon. members who have preceded me in supporting this intiative on the part of the government to increase the minimum wage rate for employees in Canada who come under the direct control of the federal government. As was pointed out by the previous speaker, it should be emphasized that this legislation will directly affect very few Canadians, roughly 7,000 out of a total of approximately half a million who are presently covered by the federal minimum wage rate legislation.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
There are certain things about this bill with which I disagree. Like the hon. member who preceded me, I hold firmly to the view that if there is to be a fairly uniform code of justice for the workers of Canada, the federal government will have to take the initiative, though I realize, of course, the federal government is limited in this respect by the con-sti ution. However, there is not much point in this government bringing in a minimum wage rate of $1.65 an hour, inadequate as it is in my opinion, although it is better than the previous rate. There is little consolation for us in supporting legislation which brings the minimum wage rate for employees under federal jurisdiction up to $1.65 an hour when we have in this country ten different standards affecting our workers.
In my province of Newfoundland we have the lowest minimum wage rate in Canada. Statistics have been placed on the record during the course of this debate which give the minimum wage rates for the various provinces of Canada. I shall not burden the House by repeating them, although repetition of this nature should serve the useful purpose of driving the point home to the minister and the government. The government must not only raise its own minimum wage rate to reasonable level-it is still not high enough-but must go further and use the influence it has with the provinces to encourage, coerce or by whatever means possible influence the provinces to raise their minimum wage rates to an acceptable standard.
The rate to be established by the bill now before us will mean that the pay of a federal government employee will amount to $66 for a 40-hour week. In this day and age of inflation which is rampant across the country, and with the cost of living taking its toll in varying degree, especially in the regionally disadvantaged areas of the country, such a wage is not enough for a man to sustain himself and his dependants. This is on the basis of $1.65 an hour, the rate proposed by this bill. What about the situation in the province of Newfoundland where the rate is set at $1.10 an hour for men and at the discriminatory figure of 85 cents an hour for women. This is in a province where the per capita cost of living is the highest in the country.
The injustice of this situation becomes readily apparent. In addition to that discriminatory rate for women, who in many instances do the same work as men, there are unjust and unfair exceptions. Up until a few weeks ago, people engaged in work in fish plants were excluded from the provincial minimum wage law. Females engaged in domestic work are still excluded from the provincial minimum wage law. Now, however, the exclusion in respect of fish plants has been eliminated.
The majority of the people who work in the fresh frozen fish plants in my province are women. They perform very hard work while standing in a chilled room, handling fish which come out of the refrigerated lockers of a ship. They work ten hours a day. Imagine working ten hours a day at a rate of 85 cents an hour and having a take-home pay for one day of $8.50! The injustice of this situation is apparent, particularly in a province where in many instances the people have to pay 45 cents or 50 cents for a quart of milk and where the ordinary means of obtaining protein through the use of beef or other meat is practically cut off because they cannot afford it. This is an injustice about which I am sure the minister is aware, because I know from his background that he does care. However, I wish he could find some way to transmit his concern and the concern of Members of Parliament to his provincial counterparts so that they would do something about provincial minimum wage rates.
We might consider for a moment the anomaly of five of the ten provinces of our country paying more in direct welfare payments than in wages under their minimum wage laws. These interesting statistics, which reveal what can be described as a paradox, were brought

May 29, 1970	COMMONS
out during the hearings of the Senate Committee on Poverty. The provinces are Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. The statistics show that the total payment for a family of four on the welfare rolls ranges from $2,100 a year in Nova Scotia to $2,953 a year in Manitoba, with Ontario coming a close second to Manitoba. Here is an area in which the federal government has a direct responsibility under the Canada Assistance Plan. This is perhaps an area wherein the federal government could use its influence with a province by saying that we can no longer continue the anomalous situation in which provincial welfare payments-which are the consequence of federal participation and in which we pick up 50 per cent of the shot-exceed the amount a worker can receive under the minimum wage law of the province.
I suggest it would be logical for the federal government to expect the provincial governments to at least bring their minimum wage rates up to a point where people would be encouraged to work rather than to sit at home and accept welfare payments. If I were working for the minimum wage in my province, and had a family of five or six and could only hope to receive the minimum wage of $3.10 an hour which would give me a take-home pay of less than $50 a week, I too would be encouraged to give up my job. As a matter of fact, I would be a fool if I did not do that, and apply for welfare, since in my province the welfare payment would exceed the weekly pay cheque I would receive as a result of my labour because of the unjust minimum wage rate which, as everybody knows, in many cases becomes the maximum wage rate. This is the type of injustice with which we live in this country. Whether we have to live with it is another question entirely.
I believe it is a waste of the taxpayers' time for we in this Parliament to speak about increasing the minimum wage rate for employees under federal jurisdiction when we know this measure will affect only half a million workers and that only 7,000 of those people will be directly affected because the vast majority of Canadians come under the jurisdiction of provincial minimum wage laws. The minister has some feelings in this regard. I know he is less enthusiastic about this legislation because of the paradoxical situation which exists all across the country.
I was not in the chamber for all the minister's speech, but I understand that we are to

I hope that the percentage rates that will be used will be in excess of those presently used for old age pensioners. I hope that plan will soon be effected. I repeat that the number of Canadians directly affected by this legislation is only a small percentage of the whole population in a country where we have a different standard for each of the ten provinces. We have different minimum wage laws and different methods of applying them.

I do not know whether a conference of provincial ministers of labour has ever taken place at the federal initiative, but the time is ripe for one to take place. This minister should use his initiative in calling such a conference to try to bring uniformity into the minimum wage laws of the country and to try to tie the minimum wage laws to a national criterion. I think the national criterion that should be used is the cost of living. It should be based on the province with the highest per capita cost of living. That is the only way in which a minimum wage can be applied across the country with any degree of justice.
I, too, am sorry to see the unjust exception of young people carried into this supposedly enlightened age. I cannot figure out, for the life of me, why we would exclude people 17 years of age and under. Many of us in this House started our working careers at an earlier age than that. Even today there is no law to protect unscrupulous entrepreneurs and companies of various types taking advantage of young people who are forced to work because of circumstances over which they have no control, young people who have to obtain employment to help sustain large families, as was my situation. I welcome this bill. I am sorry that it does not propose $2 an hour because I think that would be a fair start. I am not as confident as the hon. gentleman who preceded me that this legislation will stir the provinces into bringing in similar increases. It has not been

Increase in Minimum Hourly Wage the case in the past and I doubt if it will be the case in the future, unless we take steps and set up the means whereby there will be a national formula, a national program so that we can have a standard right across this country to ensure that Canadians, whether they are working in St. John's, Newfoundland, or Saskatoon, Saska'.chewan, will receive justice and will be guaranteed enough take-home pay to sustain them and their dependants.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for their courtesy in permitting me to bring the debate to an end at a rather early hour this afternoon. I was particularly pleased at the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) in welcoming me back to the House and pointing out that on a previous occasion when I had intended to bring in legislation I was called away at the last moment through illness. I could not help recalling, when he spoke about my recent illness, one of the favourite expressions of the late Premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, who said whenever one alluded to his health, "I am dangerously well".
I was very impressed by all the contributions, particularly that of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who in wrapping up for his party the whole problem of poverty in this country indicated a feeling which I can understand and which I think is felt by more people, regardless of their background, than we realize. It is true that when I started work my salary amounted to 30 cents an hour, which I am almost ashamed to mention these days. It was $12 a week. I remember that my pay when I married and worked on the railways was 79 cents an hour, roughly $32 a week, because I think one got an extra cent an hour if one happened to be there and punched the clock on time in the morning, not my strongest suit, I am afraid.
There has been a tendency here this afternoon to look on a standard minimum wage as the only solution in the fight against poverty.
I am sure that this is unintentional. It is one of the many tools at the disposal not only of the federal government but of provincial governments in the fight against poverty. I think this has been a common theme in all the speeches that have been made today from all parts of the House. We all have a growing 
apprehension of increasing poverty because of the high rate of unemployment in this country.
I sensed, from what most hon. members said, the realization of the need for a greater degree of co-operation between the federal departments and their provincial counterparts in order that we make the war against poverty as fruitful and as effective as possible. The suggestion that I meet with the provincial ministers of labour is, of course, a very progressive one. I say that after having the experience of initiating such a move last year. I well remember the suspicion of some of the ministers, when we called the meeting, as to what I was out to sell them. But we established a very healthy and happy relationship early in the meeting when it became apparent to all of us that the purpose of the meeting was to exchange ideas and experiences.
I think on balance I left the meeting a much wiser Minister of Labour than when I first attended because the ministers of labour of many of our provinces, regardless of their political background, brought a great depth of experience to the conference. We were able to review, for instance, the Woods task force report and find out that many of the provinces are further ahead than the federal government in the implementation of some of its recommendations.
I say that the minimum wage is only one of a number of steps to be taken to fight poverty. I think another point that the hon. member for St. John's East made quite forcibly, and which is all too often forgotten in this country, is that there is a very mistaken conception about the cost of living across Canada. To the people in the Atlantic provinces the cost of living is much lower than the cost of living in large metropolitan areas such as Montreal and Toronto. As the hon. member pointed out, this is due to geography and the high cost of transportation. But where or not there are reasons for it, this is small consolation to a person who must live on a provincial minimum wage of $1.10 or 85 cents an hour. I think we have to look at the minimum wage in the context of the other programs that are available. We have to look at it, for instance, in the context of an overall fight to remove disparity to as great a degree as possible. As the hon. member for St. John's East said, the cost of living is almost uniform across this country but the advantages of being a Canadian are not equal. The
May 29, 1970	COMMONS
pockets of poverty which we dismiss all too easily for geographic reasons are no longer acceptable to many Canadians.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Coupled with objective and effective legislation on a minimum wage must come a greater rationalization of certain industries. The textile industry is a good example of where inefficiency has been permitted to exist for too long. Because it is a labour-incentive industry it has been able to survive and compete to a degree behind a high tariff wall and lower than average wages. Two or three weeks ago, in announcing a new textile policy the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) made it quite clear that over the next couple of years ra ionalization in the tex'ile industry will permit that industry to become more automated. That is not a word to fear. The textile industry must accept technological change and the unions must accept disruption caused by jurisdictional conflicts.
Out of this rationalization should come a viable industry, one better equipped to compete with the other textile manufacturing countries of the world. It should then be able to support better paid workers who will no longer be relying on federal or minimum wage standards to bring home any kind of tolerable wage. This, of course, must happen and is happening to some degree in the fishing industry under legislation which the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) has proposed or is about to propose.
As I said earlier Mr. Speaker, having reviewed the Labour (Standards) Code I found the main defect in our approach to the minimum wage at the federal level was not in the amount but perhaps was in the very logical point made by the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys. It has been five years since the last increase. In fact, it has been five years since the bill was incorporated, and that was the first time in federal history that we had any minimum standard. I thought perhaps this was more significant, in the last analysis, than the amount. If a minimum wage is to have its major impact on the economy in the sense that it helps to redistribute the economy, it should be something that is adjusted annually.
As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker-and the House can take this as the word of the Minister of Labour-in the fall when the Labour (Standards) Code comes forward it will include provisions that will make it pos-
DEBATES	7507
Increase in Minimum Hourly Wage sible to adjust the minimum wage automatically every year. Furthermore, that increase will not be a hit and miss affair but will be based on a formula that goes beyond just the cost of living as is suggested here. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) mentioned, this would perpetuate poverty and would never close the gap.
The formula used in arriving at $1.65 an hour from $1.25 was a culmination of the cost of living index and the productivity index. If we had used the cost of living index alone, we would have arrived at a figure between $1.45 and $1.50. By adding the productivity index we were able to come to the figure of $1.65, which is about 6 per cent more per annum since 1965. For these reasons, Mr. speaker, I am more insistent on the importance of an annual increase rather than one just when the House gets down to it. We do get unforeseen events such as elections and other things that sometimes make it impossible to act on schedule.
According to the formula I have in mind there will be at least an annual increase in the minimum wage. Some of the economists to whom I have spoken approve the minimum wage as a weapon against poverty. Those who do not, claim that one of the reasons it is ineffective is that it is so seldom raised. I think we can remove this objection by finding a formula that will be predictable in the amount of increase, perhaps once a year in July tied in with a formula that goes beyond the cost of living index. I have not forgotten the question of salary increases across the country as one of the indexes.
Perhaps earlier I should have spoken a little more elaborately on the question of people under the age of 17 whose rate is set by regulation at the present time. The philosophy behind that proposal was that we did not want to neutralize other incentives. The desirable social goal in 1965 was to make sure that as many as possible under the age of 17 would remain in high school or university and that only those who were motivated by reasons beyond their control would be induced into the work force by what appeared to be attractive wages. Regulation provides some flexibility and it is my intention to increase the minimum wage for people under 17 in the same proportion or perhaps by the same amount.
I have the same attitude toward people who are handicapped mentally to some degree and physically. We have not forgotten the young people. I am just repeating, as requested, the
May 29, 1970

Increase in Minimum Hourly Wage philosophy for not establishing a minimum wage in 1965 for people under 17. We believe that wherever possible our whole effort should be directed toward fighting the war on poverty and that we should help those who have traditionally been handicapped by a lack of education. The Senate Committee hearings have been extremely valuable in pointing out the pattern with which these people inevitably or all too frequently conform. People with a minimum education usually come from the lower-income brackets, if for no other reason than that there is no incentive or opportunity for them to obtain a better education.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be able to do much in the field of vocational training through programs in certain parts of the country. There are other programs, such as textile rationalization. The battle against poverty must be won, not strictly through minimum wages by trying to provide what is considered a liveable wage but by eliminating the whole problem by a concentrated and co-ordinated effort in all existing programs. The hon. member for St. John's East pointed out one of the weaknesses in our approach, that of insufficient co-operation and co-ordination in the past with our provincial counterparts to do something about the degrading problem of poverty.
I could defend the $1.65 minimum wage- indeed, I think I am doing just that-simply because I do not regard it as the only tool to combat poverty but only one of the many. As I said, I am satisfied that introducing the annual increase to the minimum wage will exert the type of pressure we want on the provinces so that they in turn will increase their minimum wage. As has been pointed out-and this was another of my considerations-a $2 level in Newfoundland or the other Atlantic provinces would have caused a real distortion in some industries to the point where so much havoc could be created that an industry would have simply moved into the centre of Canada where it was closer to the market and had the advantage of a lower wage package; alternatively, it might switch to automation. So there are delicate balances in arriving at a figure. I have no illusions, Mr. Speaker, that if I had come in with a $2 an hour minimum wage someone would have suggested it should be $2.25.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I gather, from having listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that he enjoys no more influence with the Premier of 
Manitoba than he does with the Minister of Labour in Ottawa. He tried to sell the $2 figure to that province but was not able to convince the Premier, who is a humanitarian at heart. Certainly he is a Liberal if he is not a Socialist. Perhaps that has been the reason for his success. He knew how far to go and did not go farther. Perhaps that is why some looked on him with suspicion. At any rate, he lives next to the province of Alberta and the minimum wage of his province is higher than that of Alberta.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Does the minister not know his geography?

I deliberately skipped the province governed by a Liberal government, for various reasons. I know their minimum wage rate. I think we exert a greater influence on the provinces than the sheer size of the federal government might imply. We use our minimum wage standards in federal contracts that are awarded for public works, for instance. We insist on minimum wages being paid in highway construction projects in those areas coming under federal jurisdiction. The minimum wages are reflected in the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, which governs minimum standards involved in the awarding of tenders. So we have a substantial and effective influence in this field.
I hope that once we have defeated future NDP amendments we shall pass the bill as quickly as possible in order to allow those enlightened employers who may have accepted this concept the opportunity to make the necessary adjustments to payrolls and to computers used in calculating wages, and so on.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the minister permit a question?

It is not about my
geography?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
It is
not about the minister's geography. Since he has referred to possible problems of computing, does he not think it would be much simpler if the computers could work with a round figure like $2 an hour instead of the awkward figure of $1.65?

Working with $2 may be much easier but it would not be realistic. Perhaps that shows the difference between myself and the hon. member. I must be realistic in what I am doing and, being realistic, I have set the minimum wage at $1.65 an hour. That is not a figure for which I apologize. It is
May 29, 1970	COMMONS
not a figure with which I have been saddled. It is one that is accepted by cabinet, and I am responsible for it. We took the $1.25 previous minimum wage, calculated the increase in the cost of living as well as the increase in national productivity during the past five years, and arrived at the figure of $1.65, a figure which has the support of my cabinet colleagues. In the fall I shall bring in some more substantial changes to the code that will enable the minimum wage rate to be adjusted annually.
This, of course, will affect all the provinces and provincial ministers of labour. We must not forget that the actions of the federal government in this field influence the provinces. It is important that we enjoy a uniform minimum wage across the country. As I said earlier, I do not believe in regional differences in the minimum wage and I do not think that the people in different parts of Canada should accept a lesser or lower rate of wages, where that is unnecessary.
Hear, hear!

I do not believe that the cost of living of the people of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia or the Maritimes generally is any lower than that of the people of central Canada, and any alleged differences in living costs are exaggerated. I often wonder why this myth has not been more forcefully dispelled in public, because the cost of living in the more remote areas of Canada is as great as it is in central Canada. There is no particular reason, therefore, why minimum wages in one end of the country should be different from those paid in the central provinces.
Hear, hear!

Certainly, I do not subscribe to the idea that living costs in those parts of the country are lower than elsewhere. That is not the basis of my thinking.
As hon. members have said, and as I have pointed out, the level of the federally set minimum wage exerts an influence on the provinces. We must be careful, therefore, not to set an unrealistic rate, because if the level is too high problems will be created for some industries in some of the provinces before they have had the opportunity to take advantage of existing programs that departments of government have put at their disposal.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), who is not here at present, raised the question of marginal industries. I suggest

Aeronautics Act Regulations Bill that most marginal industries in this country of the kind the hon. member alluded to ought to take a second look at some of the programs available from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. They should take advantage of assistance offered, rationalize operations, take advantage of financial assistance and the advice of experts in the field and introduce technological changes which will make them more competitive and enable them to rely less on the payment of starvation wages in order to survive.
In conclusion, I thank the House for its courtesy. I hope hon. members will co-operate in the various stages the bill must pass through before it becomes law.

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer relations with the former British possessions in the West Indies which have not yet attained independence and further that, if the residents of these islands so desire it, economic and political union of these islands with the Dominion of Canada be negotiated at an early date at the proper constitutional levels.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as one who tries to appear as young as possible, I am reluctant to point out that this is the fourth time in recent years that I have presented this particular resolution or one in similar terms. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the halfcentury mark can give the semblance of having fun at 50, possibly I can appear something less than a geronton among the group here.
This nation's foreign policy may very properly be judged by its success or failure in dealing with the neighbouring communities to which this motion refers. There are many reasons why Canada should be especially interested in the Commonwealth Caribbean, reasons more profound than those of some of us, like my colleagues to the right, who have a fondness for rum and other derivatives of molasses and sugar which come from that part of the world.

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext: Speak for yourself.

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
There are many reasons why Canada should be interested in the Commonwealth Caribbean. It has pained me greatly that in recent months, and in particular in recent weeks, we seemed to have failed to strengthen our ties with these people or to retain the good will which we once had with the people of the Commonwealth Caribbean. In fact, we have lost esteem and regard in this area, an area which in my opinion must be one of major concern and high priority.
A few days ago I read an article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald by a leading expert in the Canadian academic field and Canada-West Indian relations, Professor Duncan Fraser. The article was headlined, "Canada-West Indian Relations Worsening". I hope

those who have responsibility in this field will carefully note and inwardly digest the pertinent comments of Professor Fraser. A most distinguished and highly informed expert on and from the West Indies recently declared before a committee of the other place:
I would say at the moment there is stronger resentment and hostility to Canada as a power than against any other power that I know of in recent years.
These are the words of Dr. George E. Eaton, professor of economics and director of professional studies, Atkinson College, York University, a native of Jamaica and a most lucid and well informed expert on West Indian affairs. It was with great sorrow that I heard the testimony of this man. Dr. Eaton's remarks are not isolated comments; they are typical of the appraisals of many thoughtful people who care about our relations with our Caribbean neighbours. While not wishing to inject excessive partisanship into the private members' hour which on Friday afternoon should be a tranquil exercise in good fellowship, I cannot but observe that the decline in our diplomacy in this area is too sadly akin to recent contractions of the Canadian role in respect of other parts of the world.
Only the most bitter partisan or the most myopic observer would deny that in our relations with the United States we have hit a new low in co-operation which fearfully may lead to a new high in disadvantage for this country when the final excesses of nationalistic bombast have been delivered. The real facts will come home to underwrite the folly of loose-lipping. Who really believes that our influence in Europe has been increased or made more meaningful in the last two years? I have not heard that testimony from any observer or authoritative person on or about the scene. Would anyone suggest, even task force personnel, that we have played even a minor role in Commonwealth affairs after the last Prime Ministers' conference and our "last-minuteism" regarding Nigeria and Biafra?
Do we play a meaningful role in the Far East? Highly publicized charismatic adventures are not diplomatic triumphs. Have we made any contribution in the Middle East? At limes it seems we are not even able to retain a balanced state of non-involvement or nonpreference in this area of non-activity. Has anyone heard recently of a major Canadian contribution to the United Nations or any of its agencies?
May 29, 1970

I am afraid in the year 1970 we are suffering from the kind of excess of non-involvement or withdrawal which distinguished the Mackenzie King era which will not go down in the annals of great statesmanship when Canadian history is finally written. Most painful of all is our failure to deal in terms of friendship and helpfulness with those people whom we should be able to understand best, our Caribbean neighbours, whose institutions in many ways are similar to ours and whose contacts with us have been close and long established.
The people in eastern Canada, the Mari-times, have had associations with the people in the West Indies, associations which have benefited both groups. Perhaps, as I said in a previous debate, they get the worst of the bargain when we send them salt cod and they send back rum. However, new dietary science has indicated that the lowly cod is in fact a highly beneficial nutritious food. The contacts between our people were valuable. It is a shame they have been lost. A more imaginative government could have done much more through the development of a seaborne commerce with these people, with the more advanced technology in reference to refrigerated ships to stimulate the trade that could exist between the two areas.
It has long been my contention that in our external aid program, to use the old-fashioned expression, we have been giving too little to too many. A country like Canada cannot mount a meaningful program of aid to nearly 70 countries flung across the globe. We must choose those areas where our aid could be effective, perhaps even decisive. In those countries it is very difficult to guarantee that Canadian aid, assistance and co-operation should command first priority.

If at another time the interjecting minister will give me an opportunity to give him a list, I will be glad to do so. Right now I am trying, as a reasonably good Member of Parliament, to stay within the terms of the resolution. When he comes forward with his Trade and Commerce estimates before the committee of the whole, I will give him some advice; but I do not think he will be doing that.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
If we cannot give meaningful help to these small islands with which we share a common heritage and generations of friendly associa-
External Affairs
tion, I wonder whether we can really do it effectively anywhere. If we fail here, ought we not to consider carefully whether or not there is a grave flaw in our exercise of programs of this type?
It is easy to point to the islands in the south and say the current coolness of attitude arises from a certain maladroilness in connection with events at Sir George Williams University. It is easy to say it is the result of excesses among black power advocates or that it is due to insensitivity on the part of some Canadian business institutions. In my view we would be less than candid and would be serving our national interests less than well if we assumed that in saying these things we were giving an adequate analysis of the situation. Much more serious, I believe, is that in this area for too long we have been too insensitive to the values of the people in the Caribbean region and we are now reaping the consequences of some of the insincerity we have shown for so many years.
Our sugar policy alone has injured their economy, and we have sharply debased our credibility by unilaterally repudiating the agreement with respect to sugar subsidies. I hear the minister of anti-Americanism, the minister in charge of resources, talking constantly about unilateral action on the part of the United States. Apparently it is perfectly in order for Canada to act unilaterally in reference to sugar subsidies-to turn away from the commitment given here in 1966 at the Caribbean Conference held in Ottawa. I think our action in this regard was totally shameful; it is one which no Canadian should accept without feelings of chagrin and shame. I quote from a recent article by Professor Fraser in which he says:
During the 1966 Canada-Commonwealth Caribbean Conference in Ottawa a West Indian cabinet minister deeply involved in negotiations for a more realistic and generous Canadian policy toward West Indian sugar assured me that he was confident that the Canadian government was about to give West Indian sugar producers the fair deal and fair prices they had long sought.
Lester Pearson's government in fact gave the West Indies a sum the equivalent to the duty collected on West Indian sugar imported into Canada of 29 cents a hundredweight.
This 29 cents has recently been unilaterally revoked by Canada.
The Professor goes on to point out that by this one act alone, Canada diminished its credibility, its popularity and its effectiveness.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Is it not true that Canada still

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext: It is true that Canada is buying sugar at a price below the price at which we indicated we would buy it. I think this is significant. It is all very well to honour commitments when the price of sugar is high. However, the defenders of unilateral repudiation will be able to explain their position as soon as I am through. If this is the new diplomacy, I want none of it. Having once given a commitment of this kind I believe we should honour it, no matter what happens to the world price of sugar. It was not geared thereto.

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
This unilateralism on our part ill-becomes a government which at times seeks to present itself as the great honourer of commitments, the great international crusader. There are always problems in these small communities, many of them serious enough to stagger their polity. They present immense challenges to the political leaders. I should like to see us declare in this Parliament that we regard these people as important and their problems as paramount, that we look upon the Caribbean area as being something more than a place where Canadians can have fun in the sun or make a few easy dollars in quick investments. Contrary to a suggestion made by a Liberal member last session, my motion does not contain any attitude of superiority or any reincarnation of colonialism. I ask that we extend to these, our neighbours, the fullest measure of goodwill and co-operation and, if they desire it, that we go even to the point of being willing to share with them a common political entity.
In eastern Canada some people, not many, are talking about maritime union. I think the project of uniting the three old maritime provinces is stillborn; I do not think it will get anywhere. But if we could include Newfoundland, with its great northern frontier, which has always since Confederation been denied the old maritime provinces, that would be a different situation. And if there were included, along with that, some of the communities of the Caribbean which might wish to throw their lot in with us, and if we had a province which to throw their lot in with us, and if we had a province which extended from Grenada to Labrador, we would have a concept which would ruffled up our spirits and give new verve to the imagination. For maritime union as now presented I am among 
the unconvinced and the unenthusiastic, but for a maritime or Atlantic province stretching from Grenada to Labrador I would be a starry-eyed zealot. Whatever the political configuration, we must move and move soon or we shall have to chalk up as a failure our activities in one of the most potentially favourable areas of our foreign policy.
So I would ask hon. members to give careful consideration to the failures which have recently been dramatised, but which are not so recent in their development, in connection with the Canadian presence in the Caribbean and the attitude of the Caribbean people toward this country. For too long Canadians have been easy and relaxed, rejoicing that they were not as other people were, notably the Americans. But here in the Caribbean, the area in which we can do the most and should be doing the most, we find that our attitudes, our aspirations and our values are being questioned. The time has come to stop taking one another for granted, to look again at this area and to question our policies. If we cannot be successful with the Commonwealth Caribbean, I think we can right write "finis to our ambition for any successful outreach in our foreign policies.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the mover of this motion, who indicated that this is the fourth time he has presented it to the House. There is no question that the debate provoked by a discussion of this motion is a most useful exercise. In my exchange with the hon. member a few minutes ago I was not seeking to engage in partisan comment with him, because without question I share the motives and objectives behind his motion.
Along with the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCuteheon) I recently had the opportunity, thanks to the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, to attend a seminar on parliamentary procedure in the United Kingdom. At that parliamentary seminar were represented a number of countries of the Caribbean, those that have achieved independence and some that expect and hope to do so in the near future. I note that the hon. member's motion deals with those countries that have not yet achieved independence. There is no question that we have to look at the economy of the Caribbean and at the problems in that area bearing in mind that this is a regional problem and that our policy must have aspects broader than merely relating to the small number of countries in
May 29, 1970

that area which have not yet achieved total independence.
Democracy in Canada as we know it is a little over 100 years old. Prior to that time there were representative institutions in the provinces and in the Atlantic seaboard. The countries of the Caribbean had representative institutions even prior to the Atlantic provinces. Indeed, they have a tradition of democratic representation of which they are properly and justly proud. Since then the evolution of those democratic institutions has assumed different forms. Today we are a nation of over 21 million, highly industrialized, with an aid program we have attempted to extend to this particular part of the world and encompassing the type of assistance that would enable the people there to achieve the kind of standard of living that every country wants to have in the twentieth century.
Where I differ from the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) who moved the motion is on the question of adjustment between Canada and the Caribbean area. I know the hon. member for Lambton-Kent and I share some close personal friendships that we had the opportunity of establishing with some mature parliamentarians who would properly be accorded a place in any Parliament in the Commonwealth. I think of men like the Speaker in St. Lucia, a very sophisticated and mature student of parliamentary procedure. I know that today these people are fighting within the Caribbean communities a battle which as recently as two or three years ago was not even a challenge to them.
The hon. member for Hillsborough painted the picture for us by quoting the view of some of those who assess Canadian development potential that our popularity in the Caribbean has changed within a short period of time. Just a little while ago we were a country to which the Caribbean was looking to replace the United Kingdom as far as external relations are concerned, to give aid in defence matters, foreign policy and national development. But today we are an imperialistic nation whose banks are attacked, whose private investment is subjected to criticism and whose motives are suspect.
There is no question that two matters in particular are a source of aggravation. The first relates to immigration. Here it seems that we cannot do the right thing. Apparently Canada attracts about 14,000 immigrants a year from the Caribbean area. These people are, generally speaking, skilled-nurses, 22375-57
External Affairs
professional people, students who have taken training in Canada and have come here under our aid program. Yet we are accused of subjecting the Caribbean to a brain drain. We are accused of robbing them of their investment in social capital. We are accused of being the kind of nation that is depriving them of the leadership they will need to achieve the kind of society that they have set as their objective.
Let us look at the other side of the coin. If Canada were not to extend aid to the countries of the Caribbean, if we were not to open our universities to them, if we were not to have a program of development equal to $24 million annually for four million people, or $6 per year for every man, woman and child in the area-contrasted with 15 cents per year for the populations of those countries in the Colombo plan-what would be the charge against us? The difficulty is that when students from this area come to Canada, take their training and spend some time here, a number of them seek permanent admission. Now, we do not want to deny them. We do not want to discriminate in our admission policy. We do not want to tell them they must go back home and serve in their own country, because it is not for us to impose that kind of decision upon them. So we will be damned if we do, and damned if we don't.
There is no easy way to make this kind of adjustment in a difficult period. As a member of this House I say without qualification that I am proud of our program and that I hope it will be extended. I hope we will do more. I also hope we will not allow the pinpricks of an incident like that at McGill to distort our objectives. As a Canadian I do not think there is anything wrong with charging any person who comes to this country and destroys property and who riots. Our courts have an obligation to enforce our laws without fear or favour, with impunity, with impartiality. When fines are assessed as a result of a proceeding before the court in which there is full process of law, I do not like the representative of another country paying those fines and thereby condoning actions which were condemned in a Canadian court. This incident will not in any way affect the attitude I take as a member of this House toward our aid program and the wish I express that it be more extensive next year than this year. Similarly, I hope our universities will accept larger numbers of students from the Caribbean area because it is here that we have a very great challenge to demonstrate what we can do.

May 29, 1970
External Affairs
The other area where difficulty has arisen is trade. My exchange with the hon. member for Hillsborough related to one aspect of trade, sugar. As I understand the background of this situation, Canada unilaterally undertook voluntarily to rebate the 29 cents per 100 pounds duty that was imposed on sugar imports. This was in anticipation of a world sugar agreement. I understand we now buy our sugar under this world sugar agreement; we do not make our purchases on the same basis as the United States or the United Kingdom. I am also given to understand that we have decided that this policy is not achieving its objective: it is not coping with the basic problem of the sugar producers in the Caribbean area. At the moment we have put in its place a $5 million development fund proposal. We have not entirely closed our minds; we are still talking about the problem.
In the minds of some, this constitutes a repudiation of an agreement, an agreement that was all one-sided. It was what we agreed we would pay and what we agreed we would do to be of help and assistance. As a Canadian I know that I have a stake in the Caribbean. I also know Canadian businesses and enterprises have a stake there of-who knows -half a billion dollars. Canadian banks have been there, along with tourist agencies, and so on.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The aluminum processing industry has a stake in bauxite processing in Jamaica. I know that the Canadian name is known and respected throughout the whole Caribbean area. I am confident that over the years it will continue to be known and respected in spite of what has been going on. The fact is that this is an area of heavy unemployment and one in which educational institutions for higher learning are lacking. It is an area of underdevelopment and one in which there are people who aspire to the good life we all want to have. It is also an area in which black power recently has made inroads. We have seen on the television screens and in many other places the demonstrations that are taking place. These are things we must expect so long as poverty and substandard conditions of life exist and so long as underdevelopment is an unfortunate but apparently inescapable fact of life in that part of the world.
There is no simple way in which a nation such as Canada, Great Britain, the United States or any one of the major industrialized
[Mr. Francis.)
areas of the world can develop its trade relations, aid programs and its representation on a voluntary basis without having certain difficulties arise. I submit that the difficulties we know now would have arisen no matter which party formed the government of our country at this time. These are difficulties of a type which is inherent in the relationship of a more mature industrialized area with an underdeveloped area.
I believe we all understand the desire for closer relationships with the countries of the Caribbean. I am completely in sympathy with the motion of the hon. member. I am under no illusion, however, that the path either in terms of our relationship with the public officials of these newly-emerging states or in respect of the public opinion of Canadians themselves will be an easy one. It will test the forebearance, tolerance, patience and longterm view of all of us.

subsubtopic: WEST INDIES-COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN- UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not in complete sympathy with the motion now before us. I should like to refresh the minds of hon. members concerning what the motion actually states. The motion is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer relations with the former British possessions in the West Indies which have not yet attained independence and further that, if the residents of these islands so desire it, economic and political union of these islands with the Dominion of Canada be negotiated at an early date at the proper constitutional levels.
I do not wish to appear to be egotistical, but I have had the privilege of being a member of this House of Commons for 17 years. As a member of the House of Commons I am not aware of any approach which has been made either through diplomatic channels or by members of the Caribbean or West Indies countries in respect of a political union with Canada. In addition, I have had the great honour and privilege during the past 14 years of being the vice-chairman of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. As such it has been my privilege to entertain as guests elected members from the Caribbean countries. Never in my 17 years as a member of the House of Commons, nor in my 14 years as vice-chairman of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, have I heard one person from the Caribbean area request political union with Canada. Therefore I just cannot understand this part of the resolution moved by the hon. member. I say it would be wrong for Canada, by the adoption
May 29, 1970

of a resolution of this kind, to take such a step. If members of the West Indies or Caribbean countries have any such thought in mind, they should approach us.
Any motion in respect of political union should come from these countries and should not come from Canada in the form of an expression of opinion from the House of Commons. Of course, I completely agree with the section dealing with economic aid. Although on occasion we may have thought we were not doing enough, I believe if we consider our assistance on a per capita, Commonwealth basis we will discover that Canada has never turned down any request for economic aid from the Caribbean nations. I am rather proud of this fact. I repeat that on a per capita basis, Canada has perhaps given more assistance than has any other nation of the world. This is my belief. If more economic aid should be required I would hope they would request it. I sincerely hope, however, that it would be done on the basis of Canada assisting the West Indies and Caribbean nations in their development rather than in the form of a double-barrelled motion which includes political union with Canada. It is up to the Caribbean nations to approach Canada in this regard; it is not up to us to pass a motion inviting them to do so. If they should make such an approach, we would consider it; we might even welcome it. But we have enough problems without expanding our dominion.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for having the forethought to bring forward the notice of motion which is before us. I am particularly taken with the second line of the motion which says that we should consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer relations with the Caribbean area and that we should consider opening our doors and giving them an invitation. In the fourth line of the motion we find the following phrase, "if the residents of these islands so desire it". I take the greatest exception to the remarks of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, because after telling us very positively how many years he had spent in the CPA and in the House of Commons he completely neglected to notice this part of the motion. If I were to invite someone to my home, I would leave to them the decision of whether or not they wished to come.
