I agree with the remarks of my friend, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis),, who commented on the conference which he-and I attended. During those four weeks we lived with many people from the Caribbean area. I admit, as did the hon. member for Hillsborough, that there are problems. But I also suggest, being an optimist, that there is a great reservoir of good will toward Canada in the Caribbean area. Of course, this good will is not increased by uninformed and unsympathetic reporting such as that found in the article which I have in my hand and from which I propose to quote extensively. It is written by Mr. Clyde Sanger, a leader writer for the Globe and Mail. The following is an excerpt:
Riots in Trinidad in March brought home to Canadians an unpleasant new fact: Canada is not seen by everyone in the Caribbean as a kindly friend and elder brother.
In fact, a strange and critical phrase began to be heard inside Ottawa's Parliament Buildings, where the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee has been studying Caribbean relations. Witnesses and Senators began talking worriedly about "a Canadian empire".
Is this exaggerated talk? It is certainly different from any ideas current here before this last year.
Eastern Canada has had close connections with the West Indies for most of a century. Schooners carrying salted cod south went first. In their wake came businessmen and bankers. The Bank of Nova Scotia has been established in Jamaica since 1889, now runs half the island's banking business.
Alcan (Aluminum Company of Canada) was the first firm to explore Jamaica's bauxite, and claims credit for semi-processing the red earth on the spot from 1952. American firms, in contrast, persisted until recently in shipping the raw bauxite immediately away.
Canadian governments-particularly that of Lester Pearson from 1963 to 1968-looked on the islands as an area of special concern. Last year development assistance to the Commonwealth Caribbean involved an allocation of $24 million.
This works out at $6 per head for the four million people there. In contrast, Canadian "aid" to Colombo Plan countries-including India, Pakistan, Ceylon and Malaysia-amounted to an average of 15 cents per person in that area.
In July 1966 Mr. Pearson held a special conference in Ottawa with a dozen heads of Caribbean governments to discuss more "fruitful collaboration."
It was all very flattering to Canada. There was hardly a cloud in the sky.
The horizon has changed dramatically in recent months. The growth of black power groups in the Caribbean is one factor. Another is the protracted trial in Montreal of students who, in the culmination of a protest against a professor's alleged racialism, first occupied and later smashed up a computer centre at Sir George Williams university.

This is the prize passage:
With extraordinary tactlessness the Canadian authorities decided to try, first of all the 97 students who had been charged (including white Canadians), a group of ten Trinidadians. The charges in Caribbean papers that Canada was more concerned about computers, and the $1.5 million damage assessed, than about human relations gained substance.
The article goes on to tell about the fire bombing in Port of Spain. Then it tells of Dr. Eric Williams' action in nationalizing the Bank of London and Montreal which, according to this article, set Canadian editors back. I quote again as follows:
The Senate committee will soon be writing its report. Since the government's white paper on Canada's foreign policy, due by June, is apparently mot going into much detail on the Caribbean, the Senate report will be exceptionally important.
But the Senators so far have failed to unearth some basic facts. Despite asking every witness, committee members are still unclear how much Canadian investment has gone into the Caribbean. They think about $500 million is there. They have no idea how much profit is being taken out-
Some Senators, too, believe it was a politically insensitive move to send Canadian infantry battalions down to Jamaica, three times during the past year, for tropical training. The Canadian chief of defence staff, General Sharp, roundly denies any idea of a secret pact with the Shearer government; but he thinks Canada should give something in return-some roadworks done by army engineers, perhaps.
Then we come to the sugar proposition. The article continues as follows:
Little has come of benefit to the Caribbean from the 1966 conference. Canada pays six pounds and ten shillings a ton above the world price for West Indian sugar-considerably less than Britain or the United States.
